common_name: Potomac Crape Myrtle (National Arboretum Medium-Pink Hybrid Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant balled or containerized stock in spring in full sun on well-drained soil, giving room for an upright, multi-trunk small tree.

directions: Potomac was bred by the U.S. National Arboretum's crape myrtle hybridizing program and carries clear medium-pink flower clusters over glossy, mildew-resistant foliage on an upright, vase-shaped small tree. Plant in full sun with good air circulation, since the fauriei parentage behind it gives strong resistance to powdery mildew compared with older straight-indica selections. Water regularly through the first growing season to establish a deep root system, then rely on rainfall except during prolonged drought. Prune only to remove dead, crossing, or low sucker growth in late winter, allowing the natural multi-trunk form and attractive exfoliating bark to develop over time.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension — Crape Myrtle Cultivar Selection

common_name: William Toovey Crape Myrtle (Classic Watermelon-Pink Heirloom Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container or balled stock in spring in full sun, choosing an open site away from structures for its eventual broad canopy.

directions: A long-grown Southern garden staple predating the mildew-resistant hybrid crape myrtles, William Toovey produces dense, semi-double clusters of vivid watermelon-pink blooms over a long summer season. Like other older straight-indica selections it can show powdery mildew in humid, still air, so give it full sun and open spacing rather than a tight foundation planting. Water deeply during establishment, then expect it to tolerate heat and drought with little supplemental irrigation once mature. Prune in late winter only to remove dead or crossing wood, since heavy topping sacrifices the natural vase-shaped form and delays the first flush of bloom.

common_name: Dallas Red Crape Myrtle (Old Reliable Dark Red Heirloom Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun on well-drained soil, giving an open site for its eventual upright, multi-trunk form.

directions: Dallas Red has been a dependable fixture of Texas and Gulf South landscapes for generations, valued for dense clusters of true dark red flowers held well above the foliage through the hottest part of summer. It performs best in full sun with good air movement, since like other older indica selections it can show some powdery mildew in shaded or humid, still conditions. Water regularly the first year or two to establish a deep root system, after which it handles heat and drought with minimal care. Limit pruning to removing dead, crossing, or low sucker growth each winter rather than cutting back hard.

common_name: Watermelon Red Crape Myrtle (Vivid Fuchsia-Red Heirloom Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun, allowing room for a broad, multi-trunk canopy to develop over time.

directions: Watermelon Red is an older straight-indica selection named for its intensely saturated, pinkish-red flower clusters, a shade brighter and more fuchsia-toned than typical crimson crape myrtle cultivars. It flowers heavily from early summer into fall on a vigorous, upright, multi-trunk shrub-to-small-tree, performing best in full sun with room for air to move through the canopy. Establish with regular watering the first season, then taper off as the deep, drought-tolerant root system matures. Keep pruning light, removing only dead or crossing wood in late winter to preserve its natural branching habit.

common_name: Royalty Crape Myrtle (Dark Violet-Purple Heirloom Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in full sun on well-drained soil, spacing to allow a dense, upright multi-stem form.

directions: Royalty is an older indica selection grown for flower clusters in a deep violet-purple rarely matched by other straight-indica cultivars, giving it a distinct place among the historic Southern heirloom crape myrtles. It forms a dense, upright, multi-stemmed shrub that works well as a large screening plant or background specimen in a full-sun border. Give it well-drained soil and consistent moisture while young, then expect good heat and drought tolerance once established. Prune in late winter to shape and remove dead wood, since it blooms on new growth and tolerates only light, infrequent renewal pruning.

common_name: Glendora White Crape Myrtle (Vigorous Old-Style White Heirloom Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in an open, full-sun site in spring, allowing generous room for a large, spreading mature canopy.

directions: Glendora White is a vigorous older straight-indica cultivar long grown for its large, pure white flower trusses on a broad, spreading tree form, and it has often served as a reference white alongside Catawba in crape myrtle breeding and mildew-resistance comparisons. Because it predates the fauriei-hybrid era it can be more prone to powdery mildew in shaded or crowded plantings, so site it in full sun with open air circulation. Water deeply through establishment, after which it tolerates heat and drought well. Prune only to remove dead, crossing, or low sucker growth in late winter, preserving the natural canopy that supports its heavy summer bloom.

common_name: Victor Crape Myrtle (Historic True Dwarf Dark Purple-Red Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Victor is one of the oldest true dwarf crape myrtle selections and needs no size-control pruning.

directions: Victor was one of the earliest true dwarf crape myrtle selections in cultivation, staying under 4 feet tall and wide with a dense, mounding habit well before compact modern series were developed. Its dark purplish-red flower clusters cover the plant through the summer, set against foliage that often takes on a reddish-bronze cast in strong sun. Grow in full sun on well-drained soil, watering regularly the first year to establish; once rooted in it tolerates heat and drought with little care. Keep pruning to the occasional removal of dead or spent wood in late winter, since its naturally compact form rarely needs size control.

common_name: Byers Wonderful White Crape Myrtle (Mississippi Nursery-Selected White Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in full sun on well-drained soil, spacing for a dense, rounded multi-stem form.

directions: Byers Wonderful White was selected by Mississippi crape myrtle growers for its heavy clusters of crisp white blooms on a dense, well-branched shrub form that holds up reliably through the Gulf Coast's long, humid summers. Its foliage shows better resistance to powdery mildew than many older white-flowered selections, making it a practical choice for a mixed shrub border or informal screen. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil and water consistently during the first season to build a strong root system. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead or crossing stems, since it blooms on new wood and needs little corrective cutting.

common_name: Black Diamond Red Hot Crape Myrtle (Dark Foliage Bright Red-Flowered Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in spring in full sun and allow room for an upright, moderately tree-like habit; Red Hot pairs the series' signature near-black foliage with the brightest red flower color in the line.

directions: Red Hot combines vivid, saturated red flower clusters with the deep maroon-to-near-black foliage that defines the Black Diamond series, giving stronger color contrast than the series' softer pink and white selections. New growth emerges coppery before darkening fully, and foliage color is most intense when the plant is grown in full sun rather than part shade. It reblooms through the Gulf Coast growing season with only light deadheading and trains easily into a single- or multi-trunk small tree form. Prune conservatively in late winter, removing dead or crossing wood only, since flowers form on new growth and heavy cutback delays the first summer flush.
sources: Southern Living Plant Collection / Black Diamond series

common_name: Country Red Crape Myrtle (Deep South Heirloom Red Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in full sun in spring, spacing for an upright, multi-trunk mature canopy.

directions: Country Red is an older straight-indica selection long favored in Deep South home landscapes for its dependable, saturated red flower clusters and vigorous, easy-care growth habit. As with other pre-hybrid indica cultivars it benefits from full sun and open spacing to minimize powdery mildew in humid conditions. Establish with regular watering through the first year or two, after which it tolerates heat, humidity, and drought with little intervention. Limit pruning to removing dead, crossing, or low sucker growth in late winter rather than topping, which delays and reduces the summer bloom flush.
